title: The lab
subtitle: Building MS-DOS 4.00 from its own source, booting it, and a FreeBSD 15.1 machine

slides.title: Two systems, one PC
slides.notes: This module sets up everything the course uses. Both systems are studied from their real source at fixed commits, and both are run, not just read.

slides.title: The lab at a glance
slides.caption: One host PC: DOSBox-X builds and boots MS-DOS 4.00; a Hyper-V Generation 1 VM runs FreeBSD 15.1
slides.notes: Left: the course repository with both source trees pinned. Top: DOSBox-X runs the 1988 toolchain over the MS-DOS source (build_dos.py), make_floppy.py writes dos400.img, and dos_run.py boots it. Bottom: the FreeBSD VM boots through the BIOS from its GPT disk; bsd_run.py reaches it over SSH and copies files, the DOS image included, with scp.

slides.title: MS-DOS 4.00 from source
slides.notes: The 2024 release includes the complete build tree with its own compilers. It does not build as published; four small problems stop it.

slides.title: The build environment the release expects
slides.code:
@echo off
echo setting up system to build the MS-DOS 4.01 SOURCE BAK...
set CL=
set LINK=
set MASM=
set COUNTRY=usa-ms
set BAKROOT=d:
rem BAKROOT points to the home drive/directory of the sources.
set LIB=%BAKROOT%\src\tools\lib
set INIT=%BAKROOT%\src\tools
set INCLUDE=%BAKROOT%\src\tools\inc
set PATH=%BAKROOT%\src\tools
callouts: tools\lib and tools\inc do not exist
The C headers and libraries are in TOOLS\BLD
slides.notes: SETENV.BAT is the official setup. Its LIB and INCLUDE paths point at folders that are not in the release; the compiler's files are under TOOLS\BLD. Our generated BUILD.BAT has the corrected paths.

slides.title: Four problems, four fixes
rows: Convert text files, detected by content
Map each back to one byte
Fixed past date on all sources
slides.notes: Each problem was found by a failing build. Line endings, character encodings, environment assumptions and make's reliance on file times: a small lesson in why a source release is not yet a build.

slides.title: The build pipeline
slides.caption: Python on the host prepares the tree and makes the floppy; the 1988 tools run inside DOSBox-X
slides.notes: Follow the arrows: prepare_dos_build.py copies the tree to build/dos4 and applies the four fixes; DOSBox-X mounts it as D: and BUILD.BAT runs one NMAKE per directory, which calls MASM, CL, LINK and EXE2BIN. build_dos.py then checks BUILD.LOG and the 62 files of CPY.BAT, make_floppy.py writes dos400.img, and dos_run.py boots it with BOOT A:.

slides.title: Why the floppy layout is not arbitrary
slides.code:
MOV     DI,BX
        MOV     CX,11
        MOV     SI,OFFSET BIO           ; point to "ibmbio  com"
        REPZ    CMPSB                   ; see if the same
        JNZ     CKERR                   ; if not there advise the user
;
; Found the BIOS.  Check the second directory entry.
;
        LEA     DI,[BX+20h]
        MOV     SI,OFFSET DOS           ; point to "ibmdos  com"
        MOV     CX,11
        REPZ    CMPSB
        JZ      DoLoad
callouts: Entry 1 must be IO.SYS, entry 2 MSDOS.SYS
Names compared as 11 bytes, as stored on disk
Then 3 sectors are read from the data start
slides.notes: MSBOOT is 512 bytes, so it assumes a lot: the first two directory entries and IO.SYS starting at the first data sector. make_floppy.py builds the image to satisfy exactly these rules, playing the role of FORMAT /S.

slides.title: The 1.44 MB lab floppy
slides.caption: IO.SYS must be directory entry 1 and start at the first data sector, sector 33
slides.notes: Walk through the arithmetic: 1 reserved sector, two FATs of 9 sectors, 14 root directory sectors, so data starts at sector 33. The boot sector checks the first two directory entries by name and reads three sectors from sector 33 without looking at the FAT. Exercise 1.1 in Module 1 decodes this boot sector byte by byte.

slides.title: Running MS-DOS 4.00
bullets: python tools/dos_run.py: boot the image and work at A:\>
With commands: run them and print their output
Output travels over COM1 into a file DOSBox-X writes
DIR *. | SORT shows two temporary files: the pipe
nasm assembles .COM programs; --file copies them in
slides.notes: Demo live: dos_run.py "DIR *. | SORT". Two zero-byte files with hexadecimal names appear in the listing. Ask the class where they come from; Module 3 answers it from TPIPE.ASM.

slides.title: How dos_run.py captures output
slides.caption: Commands go in through a temporary AUTOEXEC.BAT; their output leaves through COM1 into a file on the host
slides.notes: dos_run.py writes a temporary AUTOEXEC.BAT that redirects each command to COM1, and tells DOSBox-X to write everything sent to COM1 into a file. After BOOT A: the machine runs only our boot sector, IO.SYS, MSDOS.SYS and COMMAND.COM. SYSINIT's messages come before AUTOEXEC.BAT and are not captured; tools/screen.asm can copy the screen to the output.

slides.title: FreeBSD 15.1
slides.notes: The FreeBSD side is a normal virtual machine, installed so that it boots through the BIOS like the DOS image does.

slides.title: The FreeBSD machine
bullets: Hyper-V Generation 1, QEMU or VirtualBox without EFI
Install from disc1.iso, UFS, automatic partitioning
pkg install git nasm gdb
git clone release/15.1.0 into /usr/src, check the commit
mdconfig and mount -t msdosfs read the DOS image
slides.notes: BIOS boot matters for Module 1, which studies boot0, boot1, boot2 and BTX. Boot code experiments go on memory disks, never on the VM's own boot disk.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Both systems are studied from pinned source and run
A source release is not a build: four fixes needed
The 1988 toolchain builds the same bytes every time
512-byte boot code dictates the disk layout
The same FAT image is read by both kernels
slides.notes: Close by connecting to Module 1: we have a disk that boots. Next we follow it from the BIOS jump to 0x7C00 all the way to COMMAND.COM and /sbin/init.
